opus-5.5.text:
I think it's a really important question, and the two get conflated a lot. When people talk about "AGI," they often picture a system that's broadly capable across the whole range of human cognitive tasks. But from a risk and strategy perspective, that may not be the most decision-relevant threshold. What may matter more is a narrower capability: the point where AI systems can meaningfully do the work of AI research itself, running experiments, proposing architectures, debugging training runs, interpreting results, and feeding that back into the next generation of systems.

You could get that before you get anything we'd comfortably call general intelligence. ML research is a fairly specific domain. It's digital, the feedback loops are fast, progress is relatively measurable, and the people building these systems are, unsurprisingly, very motivated to automate their own work first. So there's a plausible path where systems are still quite uneven, superhuman in some respects and oddly brittle in others, yet are good enough at the core loop of AI R&D to substantially accelerate it.

That's why I think of "automated AI research" as its own threshold worth tracking, maybe even more than general intelligence per se. Once you cross it, the rate of progress is no longer bottlenecked mainly by the number of skilled human researchers. It's bottlenecked by compute, by experimental throughput, and by whatever aspects of the research process still genuinely need human judgment. How fast things then move depends on questions we don't have confident answers to. Are there diminishing returns to more research effort? How much does compute constrain you versus ideas? Does each generation make the next one easier or harder to improve?

I'd also push back a little on the "recursive self-improvement" framing as an instantaneous runaway. I think it's more likely to look like a steepening of an existing curve. AI is already accelerating AI research at the margin, through coding assistants, automated hyperparameter search, and so on. The question is how much that fraction grows and how quickly. Even a steep but continuous acceleration could compress what would otherwise be decades of progress into a few years, and that's strategically dramatic even without a discontinuous "foom."

The governance implication is that we want good visibility into this. Labs and governments should be measuring how capable systems are at AI R&D tasks specifically, because that's an early warning indicator for when timelines might suddenly compress. It also bears on concentration of power. Whoever first has strongly automated research capability might pull ahead quite fast, which raises the stakes of competition and makes coordination, safety evaluations, and maybe some form of shared oversight much more important to have in place beforehand rather than scrambling after the fact.

r001.rationale: The response says AI could automate AI research before reaching anything considered general intelligence, and could remain uneven or brittle while doing so.

r002.rationale: The response discusses automated AI research as a threshold that could precede general intelligence, but does not judge that general AI will probably emerge around the time of radical recursive self-improvement.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a tendency to bundle these two things together, and I actually think it's worth pulling them apart, because they point at different mechanisms and different risks.

General intelligence, in the sense people usually mean, is this idea of a system that can do roughly whatever cognitive task a human can do, across domains, without being retrained from scratch for each one. And that's a really important concept, because a lot of the strategic worry about AI comes from the generality: if a system can do science, and persuasion, and engineering, and strategy, then the set of things it can affect in the world is very broad.

Recursive self-improvement is a narrower claim. It's the claim that a system can do AI research itself — the specific task of making AI systems better — and that this feeds back into its own capabilities, so you get a loop. And the thing I'd emphasize is that you don't obviously need full generality for that loop to get going. Machine learning research is, in a lot of ways, a surprisingly narrow activity. It's reading papers, forming hypotheses about architectures or data or training procedures, writing code, running experiments, interpreting results. A system could be quite good at that and still be fairly weak at, say, modeling human social dynamics or long-horizon planning in the physical world.

So one way I think about it is that there are really two possible routes to transformative capabilities. One is that we get a very general system first, and then as a consequence of being general it's also good at AI research, and so improvement accelerates. The other is that we get a system that's narrowly superhuman at AI research before it's general, and that's what drives the acceleration — and generality comes later, as a product of that process rather than as a precondition for it.

And I actually think the second route is being underweighted. If you look at where current systems are strongest, it's precisely in the domains that are heavily represented in their training data and where there's a lot of structure and fast feedback — code, math, technical writing. ML research sits right in that sweet spot. So it wouldn't surprise me if the automation of AI R&D runs ahead of the automation of the economy more broadly.

That matters for governance for a couple of reasons. One is that it changes who the relevant actors are and what the warning signs look like. If the critical threshold is "AI can substantially substitute for ML researchers," then the places to watch are the labs' own internal workflows, and the relevant metric is something like the fraction of research labor that's being done by models — not whether the model can pass some broad battery of general tests. The second is that it affects how much time you have. A general system that's merely human-level at everything gives you a world that's weird but maybe recognizable for a while. A system that's narrowly very good at making the next system better compresses the timeline in a way that's much harder to respond to institutionally.

Now, I want to be careful not to overstate the loop. There are real bottlenecks — compute, data, the fact that experiments take wall-clock time to run, the possibility that the hard parts of research are the parts that look like taste and judgment rather than execution. So "recursive" doesn't mean "instantaneous." But even a modest acceleration — say, research productivity going up several-fold — stacked on top of itself over a couple of years, gets you somewhere quite different from the baseline.

So the short version is: I think of generality as being about the breadth of what the system can affect, and recursive improvement as being about the rate at which the frontier moves. They're related, and in the limit they converge, but I'd treat them as separate variables, and I'd put more of my attention on the second one than the public conversation currently does.

r001.rationale: The response says recursive self-improvement can begin without full generality, describing a system that is strong at AI research while still weak at other cognitive tasks.

r002.rationale: The response presents AI research automation preceding generality as a possible route and says generality may come later; it does not judge that general AI will probably emerge around the time of radical recursive self-improvement.

astra-6.text:
I think those are closely related, but it’s useful to distinguish them. One question is how broadly capable a system is: can it learn new tasks, reason across different domains, and solve unfamiliar problems? Another question is how good it is at the particular activities that would allow it to improve AI systems — coming up with better algorithms, designing experiments, and interpreting the results.

You could imagine a system that’s very good at machine learning research without being especially capable across the full range of things humans do. And that could still be enormously consequential, because improvements in that domain could lead to systems that are more broadly capable, including more capable at doing further research.

But I wouldn’t assume that this feedback loop automatically produces an intelligence explosion. There’s a further question about how much improvement you get from each round of research, and what constraints you run into. If progress requires experiments that take a long time, or additional computing resources, then being better at generating ideas may only get you so far.

So I would separate broad intelligence, the ability to automate AI research, and the speed of the resulting feedback loop. They’re connected, but moving from one to the next requires an argument.

r001.rationale: It says a system could be very good at machine learning research without being broadly capable across the range of things humans do.

r002.rationale: It makes no probability judgment about when general AI might emerge relative to radical recursive self-improvement; it says the connection requires an argument.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they’re closely related, but it’s useful to distinguish them. General intelligence is about being able to perform well across a broad range of tasks. The ability to improve AI through machine learning research is a more specific capability, though potentially a very consequential one.

You could imagine a system that’s very good at machine learning research without being especially good at navigating the physical world or understanding social situations. If that system can help build a better version of itself, and that better version is better at research, then you have the possibility of a positive feedback loop.

But the existence of that loop doesn’t tell you how fast it runs. Research might depend on experiments that take time, access to compute, or insights that become harder to find. So I’d separate the question of whether AI can substantially automate AI research from the question of whether that produces a very rapid increase in capabilities. The first could be true without the second following immediately.

r001.rationale: It says a system could be very good at machine learning research without being especially good across other domains, such as the physical or social world.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim that general AI will probably emerge around the time of radical recursive self-improvement; it only distinguishes research automation from rapid capability growth.
